analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license and a recorded sale to own or transfer a handgun or semiautomatic rifle.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2024 with two Democratic cosponsors, was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and died there without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal license, good for five years, that anyone would need to own a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that accepts a detachable magazine. Buyers would apply with fingerprints, a photo, and a background check, and every sale or transfer would have to go through a licensed dealer and be reported to a federal record-of-sale system. It also would have required owners to report lost or stolen guns and set penalties for leaving guns where children can reach them.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities that lose the most to gun violence. The bill's own findings note that Black and Latino children and teens die of gun violence at higher rates than white children, and that guns are used in roughly three-quarters of homicides. Police would also gain a paper trail: every sale of a covered gun would be reported to a federal record system with the gun's serial number and the buyer's license number, making tracing faster. Owners who follow the rules would keep their guns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities most affected by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal firearm owner license, valid for five years, required to possess a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine. Applicants submit a photo, rolled fingerprints, and personal history, and the Attorney General must run a fingerprint-based nationwide criminal background check before issuing the card, which carries the holder's photo and identifying details.

Establishes a federal record of sale: within 14 days of a transfer, the licensed dealer handling it must report the gun's make, model, and serial number, the buyer's license number, and the seller's name and address to the Attorney General, giving police a complete chain for tracing crime guns.

Closes the private-sale gap: with narrow family and emergency exceptions, any transfer of a covered firearm between unlicensed people must first go through a licensed dealer, who verifies the buyer's license is valid — effectively a background check and license check on every sale.

Adds enforcement tools aimed at everyday dangers: owners must report a lost or stolen covered firearm within 72 hours, adults can face up to five years in prison if a child accesses a loaded gun and someone is killed or seriously hurt, and dealers can face up to 10 years for failing to keep required records.

Keeps costs low for owners: the license fee is capped at $10, set only to cover the program's administrative costs, and states with their own certified licensing and record systems can run the process instead of the federal government.

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of current handgun and semiautomatic rifle owners, who would have one to two years to get a federal license (photo, fingerprints, background check, mental-health history disclosures) or face up to 10 years in prison for possessing their guns unlicensed. Buyers and sellers of used guns would pay dealer transfer fees and wait on every private sale. Licensed dealers take on new recordkeeping and 14-day reporting duties, and the Justice Department would build and run the record-of-sale system and issue regulations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun and rifle owners, dealers, and the Justice Department

drawbacks.text: Possessing a covered firearm without a license would be a crime carrying up to 10 years in prison, and existing owners would have only two years after enactment to obtain one — a serious federal penalty attached to instruments that tens of millions of Americans already own legally.

The bill strikes the existing federal statute that bars the Justice Department from establishing a system of registering firearms, and its record-of-sale database would hold serial numbers tied to buyer license numbers and seller names and addresses. Supporters point to the bill's own language denying it authorizes a 'national firearms registry,' but the practical effect is a federal list of covered gun transfers.

Every private sale or transfer — even between neighbors or strangers online — must first pass through a licensed dealer, adding dealer fees, travel, and waiting time to transactions that are currently legal with no paperwork.

Applicants must authorize release of their mental health records and are barred from licensing for five years after any stay in a mental health facility (unless they obtain a qualifying evaluation), rules that could discourage some people from seeking inpatient care.

A licensing requirement falls hardest on lower-income and rural owners who live far from dealers and licensing offices, and any paperwork error — such as failing to report an address change within 60 days — would be a federal crime.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem — guns used in roughly three-quarters of homicides, with no federal record of who owns most of them — and its tracing, loss-theft reporting, and child-access provisions are modest, well-tested ideas. But the cost side is heavy and falls on ordinary people: a near-universal federal license for handgun and semiautomatic rifle ownership, criminal penalties up to 10 years for noncompliance, dealer-mediated private sales, and a federal transfer database created by deleting the statutory ban on firearms registration. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the licensing-and-registry core is the most sweeping federal gun-ownership requirement ever proposed, that it faced near-zero political support (two cosponsors in a 435-member House), and that lighter versions — universal background checks, secure storage laws — have attracted broader backing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jonathan Jackson introduced the bill on May 10, 2024, joined by Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton as an original cosponsor, for a total of two Democratic cosponsors in the 435-member House.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, the committee that handles firearms law.

The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill under the rule that unfinished bills die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Current gun owners and the firearms industry are better off: no federal license, transfer paperwork, or record-of-sale reporting was ever imposed. Gun-rights groups also avoided a precedent by seeing the most sweeping federal licensing proposal die without a fight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Current gun owners and the firearms industry

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill; the Republican-run Judiciary Committee and House majority never moved it, so the fight never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill makes dealers the mandatory checkpoint for every sale of a covered gun, with 14-day reporting of each transfer and up to 10 years in prison for recordkeeping failures, while manufacturers face federal inspections and disclosure of production and sales figures. The industry avoided all of this when the bill died in committee.

By requiring every private transfer to run through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license, the bill would have made dealers the permanent gatekeepers of the legal gun market — new business in the form of transfer fees, but also new paperwork, inspection exposure, and criminal liability.

industries.industry: Gun owners (a large diffuse constituency, not an industry)
industries.note: Roughly tens of millions of handgun and semiautomatic rifle owners would have needed a federal license, fingerprints, and mental-health history disclosures to keep guns they already own, and would have committed a federal crime by failing to report a lost gun or an address change on time.
